speaker: rexdavis
text: Rex. There's two things that I would ask the paralegal folks to do. One is to be as technologically sophisticated as you can be because that's the world in which you live. I'm a member of the Supreme Court Rules Advisory Committee, and what that committee does, it's a committee of 50 jurists from across the state, both private practitioners, appellate specialists, academicians, judges, broad spectrum of the legal community, and we advise the Texas Supreme Court regarding the adoption and, I guess you'd say, recommended form of rules, and so that meeting, that committee met on Friday, and the Chief Justice of the Texas Supreme Court has, ever since I've been on the committee, been the liaison between the court and that group, and he always gets a little bit of opportunity to chat right at the beginning, kind of introduce the subject for the day, and one of the things that he said is that last year in Texas, the year before COVID, that we tried about, I think he said 5,000 to 6,000 cases, and I don't remember the exact number, but to a jury verdict in the state of Texas, and that about 60% of those were in Class C misdemeanor cases, meaning tried to municipal judges and or to JPs, and basically we're talking about traffic-level offenses, and you think about that, that there's that many, and that has been the one area where we have already been successful in holding entirely virtual jury trials. That means that the jurors are at home or at some location where they have technology, the attorneys are somewhere likewise, the parties are likewise, the witnesses are, and the judge are. None of those people are in the same room. When you think about the cost of moving those, say, 3,000, 4,000 cases from trying to get all those people to physically come together in a room at one time versus the ability to take a patrolman who stopped that car and have him sit in his squad car but be a witness in a trial while he's on duty, yes, the tremendous amount of savings that we have realized as a result of being forced to use this platform will make it where we resist going backwards to the physical room technology, their methodology. Now, the kinds of cases that we typically see are not the Class C misdemeanor jury trial cases. You all saw arguments in some of those cases. Just as an example, I'm gonna pick on the BSR case, not for any reason other than y'all saw that. That's an interim proceeding. The discovery in that case is deep. It is complex. It involves experts. There will be a lot of witnesses if that case is ultimately tried. And what I'm trying to say is that that kind of case, I doubt that it will ever move to an entirely virtual platform. One, it's too long. The ability of a jury to stay focused on a Zoom trial of that length would almost be impossible. They say that about three hours is really a juror's limit on the ability to concentrate but at the same time, the shorter trials, medium trials, I can see some criminal cases going to the virtual platform I mean, because especially in the short term, we haven't seen that so much yet. Actually, Brazos County is one of the counties that's kind of leading the charge on getting back into that and Rex may have more insight on that than I but I mean, trying to do vortire with a juror in a face mask or a face covering of any type, they've gone to face shields so that they can see the juror's reaction because of the need to see the body language. But the number of hearings that are being conducted via Zoom is astronomical. I forget the numbers that the chief gave us but it was in the tens of thousands of hearings that have already been conducted on Zoom and I'd kind of like John's input on this but as a trial judge, whether or not he thinks we're gonna lose a step in doing that but the ability to quickly have a hearing rather than spend so much time getting one scheduled and set up, I can see this as being a real motivator, I guess you would say, of driving down the cost of litigation in the developmental stage because you can quickly get trial court input into issues. So I think that being forced into the technology we are going to be somewhat reluctant to give it up. John, what do you think as a trial judge?

speaker: johnneill
text: I agree with most of what you said. I think uncontested hearings, non-evidentiary hearings, non-evidentiary hearings are motion for summary judgment for example, where there's no testimony taken, there's no witnesses presented, it's basically attorneys arguing to the judge their position. Uncontested hearings meaning, I did a lot of family law on the bench meaning husband and wife have reached an agreement with regards to the division of their property and custody and things like that of their children. Most of the trial courts, even if mom and dad or husband and wife do reach an agreement, most trial courts require one party or the other to come into court and provide testimony as to jurisdiction, the terms of their agreement and so forth. To me, there's no reason at all not to do that by Zoom, there's no reason at all not to have contested non-evidentiary hearings by Zoom. When I was on the bench, I was in Cleburne, north of here, Johnson County joins Tarrant County, so we had a lot of Tarrant County lawyers come down for family law and a lot of Dallas County attorneys come down for family law. And it didn't, now that Zoom is in place, like Chief says, now that it's in place, it just doesn't make sense to go backwards and say, okay, I'm gonna, my attorney's gonna charge me $300 an hour to come from Dallas just to do a simple prove-up divorce and then go back, three hours of work, $1,000, when you can do it literally in five minutes on Zoom. It just really doesn't make sense to me to go back. I see a lot more problems and difficulty with contested evidentiary hearings in trials and things like that, but a lot of what trial judges do, a lot of what trial judges do, it just doesn't get the publicity of the jury trial, but a lot of what we do are non-evidentiary contested hearings and agreed prove-ups of different types. And I think those lend themselves perfectly to Zoom hearings.
